theme_note: These codes share Chibi videos or their source as material for the subreddit’s April Fool activity; what varies is whether the contribution opens the thread, identifies its unofficial source, adds another MV, or offers a later example.

second_order: working out whether Chibi mode is real or could stay
theme_note: Participants ask whether the chibis are a real game mode, imagine replacing or supplementing existing modes, answer that the material is modded and limited, thank the answer, or resist letting it go.

second_order: joking about how the chibis look
theme_note: These codes make the chibis’ odd or mixed appearance into the activity: questioning proportions, exaggerating them, and calling the result both terrifying and adorable.

second_order: asking to keep or extend the Megane changes
theme_note: Participants press the temporary makeover beyond its initial form or date by requesting glasses on more banner figures, asking that flairs, icons or the loading gif stay, and seeking downloads; requests vary in target and politeness.

second_order: celebrating 4k Producers and thanking the room
theme_note: These codes turn the subscriber count into a shared celebration, distinguish it from the April Fool joke, thank moderators and contributors, express belonging, and call for further growth; what varies is whether speakers credit people, the room’s helpfulness, or their own attachment.
One participant recalls mistaking a username for a blog owner and the other explains that the name was chosen without knowing the site; the two turns jointly clear up the mix-up.

second_order: turning a tears misreading into a nightmare joke
theme_note: A reader turns tears into tearing a face, and the reply carries that reading into a nightmare punchline.

second_order: setting up a small Akane build
theme_note: The post and early replies scale the drawing to the room, choose Akane and a workable location, provide a live guide, set placement and color instructions, reject bots, and avoid positions the room cannot hold; the choices vary between design, tool, method and territory.

second_order: directing and doing Akane’s pixel work
theme_note: Participants ask where to begin, call others to particular parts, report joining and progress, correct their own pixels, focus effort, defend completed lines and stop damaging dots; what varies is whether a turn directs, performs, checks or reports the work.

second_order: working out overlapping claims around Akane
theme_note: These codes handle other pictures and groups occupying the same area by avoiding, contacting, warning, bargaining, shifting, persisting, fighting or making peace; the practice is working out who can use contested pixels, while its methods range from cooperation to attrition.

second_order: deciding whether to add an im@s mark
theme_note: A nearly finished Akane raises the lack of room for a label, one proposed mark is rejected for its other meaning, and the room accepts im@s instead.

The end notice, thanks, pride and final-picture remarks celebrate that the room completed Akane; speakers vary between announcing success, thanking helpers, crediting twelve hours of organizing and admiring the final canvas.
Two turns in different threads remember concrete cleaning and repair work on Akane near the end, one immediately after placement closed and one in the later retrospective.
A single post-success turn converts the last-minute build into a proposal to gather support earlier if the event returns.

second_order: making Akane’s article screenshot into a retrospective
theme_note: The later thread shares and interprets an article image centered on Akane: participants claim lasting visibility, dispute the article’s framing, congratulate or explain abstention, and joke about neighboring figures; the common practice is looking back through that screenshot, not agreement on one evaluation.
